design_detail: Systematic review with random-effects meta-analyses of proportions (Stata metaprop with the Freeman–Tukey double arcsine transformation; meta-regression on the logit scale) of studies done in Iran on tramadol use, regular use and dependence, poisoning, seizures and deaths, searched to June 2019 in PubMed (Medline), Scopus, Web of Science and the Persian Scientific Information Database (SID), with expert contacts, unpublished data (including national forensic statistics from Iran's Legal Medicine Organization) and reference lists. Not preregistered; the authors call the analysis exploratory. 84 studies: 18 on the prevalence of use, 6 on regular use and dependence, and 62 on poisoning, seizures or deaths (46 hospital or poison-centre series and other clinical datasets, 7 forensic or mortality datasets, 9 case reports); none measured poisoning or death among people who use tramadol.
can_establish: How common self-reported tramadol use was in the Iranian surveys available up to 2019 (by sex, in households, students and groups at high risk), what share of poisoning admissions, seizure presentations and drug-poisoning death records in Iranian hospital and forensic series involved tramadol, and how often seizures and deaths were recorded among people admitted to Iranian hospitals with tramadol poisoning.
cannot_establish: The risk of poisoning, seizures or death for a person who uses tramadol (no included study measured it, as the authors state); whether tramadol alone caused the recorded seizures and deaths (co-ingestion was common and toxicological confirmation was not extracted); changes over time or the effect of Iran's 2007 control measures (no before–after analysis); or figures for other countries (all studies are Iranian, and the Iranian seizure frequencies are about three times those of Australian and US series).

sample.recruitment: Database search up to June 2019 (235 records from the international databases and 203 from SID), plus 12 studies from expert contacts and 8 from reference lists; 64 database records were included after screening, giving 84 studies (PDF p. 7; Figure 1, p. 3). No limits except excluding non-human studies (PDF p. 2). Primary studies: household surveys (a national survey of 15–64-year-olds and an unpublished cohort of 15–34-year-olds in three cities), student surveys, national surveys of people who use illicit drugs, prisoners and people who inject drugs, a pharmacy-customer study, treatment-centre data, hospital and poison-centre case series, forensic death records and national adverse-reaction reports.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: studies from Iran with data on the prevalence of tramadol use, frequent or regular use and dependence, or tramadol-related poisoning, seizures or deaths. Excluded: no defined target indicator; interventional studies; tramadol data not separable from other drugs (PDF p. 2, Search strategy and selection criteria, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs). 14 full texts were excluded (8 tramadol combined with other drugs, 3 no defined indicator, 2 interventional, 1 duplicate data; Figure 1).
sample.demographics: Prevalence studies were done in 2006–2018 in 8 of the 31 provinces plus national surveys (PDF p. 25); general-population samples totalled 12,783 and student samples 17,514 (49.6% female) (PDF pp. 7–8). Poisoning series came from 17 of 31 provinces, one national (PDF p. 21), mostly 2004–2017; mean age 22.0–28.4 years with men predominating (PDF p. 23), apart from a paediatric series (mean age 3.7) and a series of women (Tables 3 and 5).
sample.selection_effects: Household prevalence data come from direct questioning that was not anonymous (Table 1, PDF p. 4: 'Direct/no'), which may under-count use, and two student estimates are indirect network scale-up estimates; the pools combine different definitions of use (non-prescribed use in 6 studies, use without medical indication in 2, any use in 8, not stated in 2). Poisoning data come from hospitals and poison centres, many in Tehran and some from the same cities and overlapping periods; people who were poisoned and not admitted are not represented.

exposure.measurement: Self-report in surveys (direct interviews or questionnaires; network scale-up in two student studies); tramadol poisoning as recorded by the hospital series (whether it was confirmed by laboratory tests is not extracted); toxicological detection in forensic records.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Use measured as lifetime, last-12-month, last-month or current use; regular use as daily or almost daily use in the last 12 months. In poisoning series, mean reported ingested amounts ranged from 363.2 to 3248 mg (study conditions; PDF p. 23); poisoning was mostly oral (Table 5).
exposure.polysubstance: In the poisoning series, tramadol-only poisonings were 43.0% to 100% of cases (several series admitted tramadol-only cases by design), and benzodiazepines were the most often named co-ingestant (Table 5); a history of other substance use or dependence was recorded in 5.3–45.9% and earlier non-medical tramadol use or dependence in 3.8–66.4% (PDF p. 23). In forensic data, opioids were co-detected in 27.4–51% of tramadol-related deaths in 2006–2008 (Table 7). The pooled estimates do not separate tramadol-only from mixed poisonings.

comparison.controls: None: single-group proportions. Men and women, populations and time frames are pooled separately; meta-regression compares study-level covariates.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The primary studies seldom recorded psychiatric history, suicide risk or other drug use in a standard way; CYP2D6 metabolizer status, which the authors invoke to explain Iran's high rates, was not measured in any included study.

outcomes.instruments: Primary-study measures: survey self-report of use; hospital records of poisoning, seizures, ICU admission and death; forensic toxicology. Quality: the Joanna Briggs Institute checklist for prevalence studies, slightly revised (Data S3), with 9 items for prevalence studies and 8 for poisoning and mortality studies, reported as the numbers of the unmet items (Tables 1 and 3).
outcomes.validity_norms: Item 6 (response rate above 70%) is counted as unmet in nearly every hospital and forensic record study (Table 3), where a response rate does not apply; no item records whether tramadol poisoning or the cause of death was confirmed by toxicology.
outcomes.operationalization: Proportions of seizures and of deaths among patients admitted with tramadol poisoning; tramadol's share of poisoning admissions, of seizure presentations and of drug-poisoning death records (labelled 'cause of death' by the review).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None (descriptive pooled proportions). 15 pooled estimates are reported in the text; Figures 2 and 3 also print overall pools across populations and time frames (8.0% for men, 1.1% for women) that are not interpreted.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Two reviewers screened, extracted and appraised independently, with a third resolving disagreements (PDF p. 2).

analysis.effect_sizes: Random-effects pooled proportions with 95% CI, I2 and, in the forest plots only, prediction intervals (PI). Last-12-month use, general population: men 4.9% (4.1–5.9; I2 61.0%; PI 1.9–9.4%), women 0.8% (0.2–1.8; I2 92.8%), women without the low-quality Tehran street study 0.5% (0.1–1.0). Lifetime use, general population (one cohort, three sites): men 15.7% (13.1–18.5), women 0.9% (0.6–1.2). Students: lifetime men 8.2% (6.5–10.1; I2 79.7%), women 1.9% (1.0–3.0; I2 87.3%); last 12 months men 4.8% (1.9–8.9; I2 95.3%; PI 0–32.3%), women 0.7% (0.3–1.1; I2 57.3%). Tramadol's share of admissions: all drug poisonings 13.1% (5.7–22.9; 3 studies; heterogeneity not reported), all-cause poisonings 4.9% (2.3–8.5; I2 99.5%; PI 0–23.5%), poisonings admitted to ICU 4.6% (3.0–6.5). Seizures among tramadol-poisoning admissions 34.6% (29.6–39.8; I2 94.0%; 23 series; PI 12.5–60.9%). Deaths among tramadol-poisoning admissions 0.7% (0.0–1.9; I2 91.7%; 18 series; PI 0–10.0%). Tramadol in drug-poisoning death records 5.7% (0.5–15.4; I2 97.6%; 4 datasets; PI 0–72.3%). Prediction intervals were read from Figures 2 and 4–7 at 300 dpi.
analysis.covariates: Meta-regression of prevalence on sex, definition of use, time frame, study year, number of unmet quality items and setting; of the poisoning share on study year and quality; of seizures on percentage of men, study year and quality; none for deaths, because one-third of the studies had no deaths (PDF p. 3). The regression tables are in Data S5, which was not read.
analysis.preregistration_detail: The authors state that the analysis was not preregistered and that the results should be considered exploratory (PDF p. 2, Data analysis). A PRISMA checklist is in Data S1.
analysis.selective_reporting: Prediction intervals are printed in the forest plots but never mentioned in the text; I2 is missing for the 13.1% drug-poisoning pool and for the general-population lifetime pools; per-study death proportions appear only in Figure 6; two series listed with seizure data in Table 5 (a paediatric series with no seizures and a series with 41.6%) are left out of the seizure pool without explanation.
analysis.power: Not addressed. Several pools rest on two to four studies; publication bias was not assessed.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In Iranian surveys up to 2019, about 5% of men and under 1% of women in households, and about 5% of male and 0.7% of female students, reported tramadol use in the past year, with use far higher among people who use illicit drugs (12.8% past year in 2018) and daily use rare in households (0.3% of men). Tramadol was involved in about 5% of all-cause and 13% of drug-poisoning admissions and in about a fifth to over half of seizure presentations in the series that measured it. Among people admitted with tramadol poisoning, a pooled 34.6% had seizures and 0.7% died, with very wide differences between hospitals (prediction intervals 12.5–60.9% and 0–10.0%).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes "tramadol use is as prevalent as the use of illicit opioids in Iran" (PDF p. 1), but no figures for illicit opioid use are analysed or shown; the comparison rests on two cited sources (PDF p. 24), and the Conclusion itself says only 'perhaps as high as' (PDF p. 25). The hundreds of tramadol-related deaths come mainly from an unpublished national dataset (336 records in 2016–17), and the Discussion calls these cases in which tramadol was the sole cause of death (PDF p. 24), which Table 7 does not show and the Limitations contradict (lack of definite confirmation of tramadol as the only or major substance, PDF p. 25). Poisonings and seizures are called 'tramadol-induced' although co-ingestion was common and confirmation was not assessed. The statement that misuse and harms have not subsided despite control policies (PDF p. 25) rests on a non-significant linear meta-regression on study year, not on any before–after comparison. The explanation by a high share of ultra-rapid CYP2D6 metabolizers in Iran (PDF p. 25) was not examined in any included study. The authors do state the absence of studies on people who use tramadol, the exploratory status of the analysis and most of the limits of the evidence.

timeline.event: Tramadol enters Iran's pharmaceutical market; adverse-reaction reports grow within months (PDF p. 2)

Iran's Ministry of Health starts control measures after rising tramadol poisonings and deaths (PDF pp. 2, 25); Iravani et al. (2010) report tramadol-related deaths in samples of forensic toxicology records rising from 0.1% in 2005 to 2.6% in 2008 (Table 7)
Talaie et al. (Tehran poison centre; seizures in 46.2% of 132 tramadol poisonings) and, earlier, Shadnia et al. (2008; 35.1% of 114), both in this review's seizure pool

Ryan and Isbister, Australian toxicology unit: seizures in 11% of 71 admissions after tramadol overdoses above 400 mg; they suggest the high Tehran frequencies may reflect patients selected for seizures
This review: the first systematic review of tramadol use and its health consequences in Iran, by the authors' account (PDF p. 25)

replication.where_it_stands: The only systematic review of tramadol use and harms in Iran among the site's sources. Its pooled seizure frequency among Iranian tramadol-poisoning admissions (34.6%) is about three times the 11% of the Australian series of Ryan and Isbister (2015), and it found no study that measured poisoning or death among people who use tramadol, so its figures describe hospital and forensic case mixes, not individual risk. Several of its pooled series come from the same cities and overlapping periods, and the review does not say whether their patients overlap.

funding.funder: Iranian National Institute for Medical Research Development (NIMAD), grant no. 940043; the funder had no role in design, implementation, analysis, interpretation or writing (PDF p. 26, Acknowledgements).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the Iranian National Center for Addiction Studies (Tehran University of Medical Sciences), Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, the Legal Medicine Organization's research centre and the Ministry of Health's Division of Pharmaceuticals and Narcotics Affairs. Several included datasets are the authors' own, some unpublished (the youth cohort [19], the national mental health survey [21] and [38], the survey of people who inject drugs [36], the treatment-centre data [40], the traffic-death study [43] and the national forensic statistics [44]), and the review team appraised them; no procedure for this is described. Recorded as a flag for closer reading.

what_would_settle_it: Linkage in Iran of tramadol dispensing records, and of repeated anonymous household surveys of non-medical use, to emergency, poisoning and death records with toxicological confirmation, giving the risk of poisoning, seizures and death per person-year of tramadol use by amount, co-ingestion and age; and a multicentre poisoning cohort with standardized seizure ascertainment, laboratory confirmation and a stated rule against counting the same patients in more than one report.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (Iran, by population group), exposure (tramadol use) and outcomes (prevalence, regular use and dependence, poisoning, seizures, deaths) are stated, as is fitting for a prevalence review.
The authors state the analysis was not preregistered and is exploratory (PDF p. 2).
Any design was accepted except interventional studies, which were excluded without a stated reason.

Three international databases and the Persian SID, key terms stated (full strategy in Data S2), no language or date limits, expert contacts, unpublished data and national forensic statistics, reference lists; the search ended in June 2019 and the paper was submitted in September 2019. No study registries were searched, which matters little for prevalence and case series.
Two reviewers screened independently, with a third resolving disagreements (PDF p. 2).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Provisional: the article says excluded studies and the reasons are listed in Data S4, which is not among the files read; Figure 1 gives counts of the 14 full-text exclusions by reason.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Tables 1, 3 and 5 give year, province, setting, sampling, response rate, data collection, age, sex, sample size, definition of use, amount and co-ingestion; the primary designs (prospective or retrospective) and how tramadol poisoning and seizures were confirmed are not described.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: A revised JBI prevalence checklist applied in duplicate, with unmet items listed per study; but the response-rate item is scored as unmet in nearly every record-based series, where it does not apply, no item covers toxicological confirmation, and no overall judgment per study is made.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported

domains.note: Random-effects pooling of proportions with a variance-stabilizing transformation, separate pools by sex, population, time frame and setting, and meta-regression for heterogeneity. Weaknesses not scored by this item: pools with I2 above 90%, possible double counting of overlapping series, and seizure and death pools that mix tramadol-only and mixed poisonings.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: Meta-regression on the number of unmet quality items (no association) and a sensitivity analysis removing studies with more than four unmet items (women in the general population: 0.8% to 0.5%).

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The Discussion and Conclusion state the pooled figures without qualifying them by the quality findings (no poisoning study met all items; three met fewer than five), and call forensic proportions 'cause of death' and 336 deaths cases of tramadol as the 'sole cause', while the Limitations note that tramadol was often not confirmed as the main substance.
I2 reported for most pools, meta-regression on several covariates, and the study site named as a likely source in the Limitations; most heterogeneity remains unexplained.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding (NIMAD) and a declaration of no interests are given; the authors' own datasets among the included studies are not flagged as such.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: AMSTAR 2 rates confidence as critically low when more than one critical item fails: here items 2 (no protocol), 13 (risk of bias not carried into the interpretation) and 15 (publication bias not considered) are 'no', item 9 is only partly met, and item 7 is provisional for want of Data S4, which cannot change the rating. This is a judgment on how far the pooled numbers can be trusted as unbiased summaries, not on the review's usefulness: it is the only systematic collection of Iranian data, with duplicate screening and extraction, a broad search including unpublished and Persian-language sources, and candid statements that no study measured individual risk. The card may be cited for the prevalence of self-reported tramadol use in the Iranian surveys, for tramadol's share of Iranian poisoning admissions, seizure presentations and death records, and for the range of seizure and death proportions among Iranian tramadol-poisoning admissions, each with its heterogeneity; not for individual risk, not for causation, and not for countries outside Iran.

key_findings.finding: 84 studies were included (64 records from the database searches and 20 from contacts or reference lists): 18 gave the prevalence of tramadol use, 6 regular use and dependence, and 62 poisoning, seizures or deaths. No study gave the frequency of poisoning or death among people who use tramadol.
key_findings.note: Figure 1 (p. 3, read on the rendered page): 438 records before duplicates were removed, 383 screened, 78 full texts assessed and 14 excluded (8 tramadol data combined with other drugs, 3 no defined indicator, 2 interventional, 1 data presented in another included study); 12 studies from contacts and 8 from reference lists. The four category counts in Figure 1 sum to 86, two more than the 84 included.

key_findings.finding: General population: lifetime use among men ranged from 13.2% to 17.8% and past-year use from 3.7% to 6.0%; among women, lifetime use 0.6–1.2% and past-year use 0.1–3.3%. Pooled lifetime use 15.7% (95% CI 13.1–18.5) in men and 0.9% (0.6–1.2) in women; pooled past-year use 4.9% (4.1–5.9; I2 61.0%) in men and 0.8% (0.2–1.8; I2 92.8%) in women, and 0.5% (0.1–1.0; I2 91.97%) in women after removing the study with more than four unmet quality items.
key_findings.locator: Results › General population, 1st paragraph (starting p. 7, continuing p. 8); Figures 2 and 3
key_findings.note: Lifetime estimates come from one unpublished cohort of 15–34-year-olds at three sites; the past-year pools add a 2011 national survey of 15–64-year-olds (n=3508) and, for women, a street-based Tehran study without a definition of use (3.3%). Prediction interval for men's past-year use, read from Figure 2: 1.9–9.4%.

key_findings.finding: University students (10 studies, total n=17,514, 49.6% female): pooled lifetime use 8.2% (6.5–10.1; I2 79.7%) in men and 1.9% (1.0–3.0; I2 87.3%) in women; pooled past-year use 4.8% (1.9–8.9; I2 95.3%) in men and 0.7% (0.3–1.1; I2 57.3%) in women. Ranges: men lifetime 5.0–17.8%, past year 1.0–11.4%; women lifetime 0–7.9%, past year 0.4–1.6%. One high-school study (Ilam): lifetime use 7.8% in boys and 1.8% in girls.
key_findings.locator: Results › Students, 1st paragraph (starting p. 8, continuing p. 13)
key_findings.note: The two highest past-year estimates for male students, 11.4% and 8.1%, are network scale-up estimates (Tables 1 and 2, pp. 4 and 6); the two national direct surveys gave 1.0% and 3.3%. Prediction interval for male students' past-year use, read from Figure 2: 0–32.3%.

key_findings.finding: The 18 prevalence studies defined use as non-prescribed use (6), use without medical indication (2) or any use (8), and 2 gave no definition; 6 met all quality items and 1 met fewer than five. In meta-regression, prevalence was lower in women (P printed as 0.000) and for the lifetime than the past-year indicator (P=0.02); definition of use, study year, unmet quality items and setting were not associated.
key_findings.locator: Results › Prevalence of tramadol use, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: High-risk groups: 14.1% lifetime non-prescribed use among 546 male prisoners (Kermanshah, 2012). People who use illicit drugs, national surveys: 2007 (n=7769), current non-prescribed use for mood change or withdrawal 26.5%, the highest of any prescription drug; 2018 (n=20,175), lifetime use 26.9%, past-year use 12.8% and daily use in the past year 2.8%. People who inject drugs in Tehran in 2006–07 (n=904, 95% men): 7.3% had injected tramadol in the past 6 months.

Regular use and dependence: in the 2011 national survey, daily or almost daily non-prescribed use in the past 12 months was reported by 0.3% of men and 0.05% of women aged 15–64, which was 5.0% of the men and 3.0% of the women who reported past-year use. Among 162 tramadol customers of seven pharmacies in one city in 2007–08 (89% under 30), 58% asked for tramadol without a prescription, 88.0% of these met the criteria for tramadol dependence, and 65.0% of all had a history of dependence on other drugs. Of 428 people admitted for drug dependence to a referral centre from 2016 to mid-2018, 6.3% sought treatment mainly for tramadol dependence (85.0% men, 37.0% under 25; 92% had started tramadol after 2007) and 31.7% had used tramadol without a prescription (74.4% starting after 2007).
key_findings.locator: Results › Regular tramadol use and dependence, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (p. 13 continuing p. 14; p. 14 continuing p. 20)
key_findings.note: The criteria used for dependence in the pharmacy study are not named.

key_findings.finding: Two Iranian case reports of tramadol withdrawal: a 30-year-old man with mental and physical symptoms 2 weeks after suddenly stopping tramadol taken for 2 years (300 mg per day, as reported), whose symptoms resolved completely within a few days; and a newborn with vomiting, poor feeding, tremor and seizures whose mother had taken tramadol for back pain during pregnancy (100 mg a day, three times a week, as reported).
key_findings.locator: Results › Regular tramadol use and dependence, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Tramadol's share of hospital poisoning admissions: 13.1% (5.7–22.9) of all drug-poisoning admissions (3 studies, n=2233), 4.9% (2.3–8.5; I2 99.5%) of all-cause poisoning admissions (5 studies, n=47,069) and 4.6% (3.0–6.5) of poisoning admissions to intensive care (2 studies, n=577); 39.0% of narcotic-poisoning admissions in one study (n=282); 20 of 1363 paediatric poisoning admissions (1.5%) over 2 years.
key_findings.locator: Table 4 (p. 14); Figure 4 (p. 20); Results › Contribution of tramadol to poisonings and seizures, 1st paragraph (starting p. 21, continuing p. 23)
key_findings.note: The three drug-poisoning studies gave 7.1%, 13.6% and 20.3% (Table 4). Read from Figure 4: I2 not estimated for the 13.1% pool; prediction interval for the all-cause pool 0–23.5%.

key_findings.finding: Tramadol's share of seizure presentations: 36.8% of all seizure cases (n=141), 21.9% of first seizures (n=383), and 39.5% and 54.7% of drug-induced seizures in two studies (n=143 and n=137).
key_findings.locator: Table 4 (p. 14); Results › Contribution of tramadol to poisonings and seizures, 2nd paragraph (p. 23)

key_findings.finding: Seizures among patients admitted with tramadol poisoning: pooled 34.6% (95% CI 29.6–39.8; I2 94.0%), ranging from 12.0% to 69.3% across studies; sex, study year and unmet quality items were not associated with seizure frequency.
key_findings.locator: Results › Seizure and mortality in tramadol poisoning, 2nd paragraph (p. 23); Figure 5 (p. 21)
key_findings.note: Read from Figure 5 at 300 dpi: 23 series pooled, prediction interval 12.5–60.9%, lowest study 11.7% (11.6% in Table 5).

key_findings.finding: Deaths among patients admitted with tramadol poisoning: nineteen studies gave mortality, ranging from 0 to 10.0% (the text adds 'in six studies'); pooled 0.7% (95% CI 0.0–1.9; I2 91.7%). All paediatric patients survived; two of the six case reports that gave an outcome ended in death.
key_findings.locator: Results › Seizure and mortality in tramadol poisoning, 2nd paragraph (p. 23); Figure 6 (p. 21)
key_findings.note: Read from Figure 6 at 300 dpi: 18 series pooled, six of them with no deaths, prediction interval 0–10.0%; the 10.0% is one Kermanshah series of 1023 patients (2008), while another Kermanshah series of 546 patients from the same years gave 0.9%.

key_findings.finding: In the 34 poisoning and seizure series, mean age ranged from 22.0 to 28.4 years and mean reported ingested amount from 363.2 to 3248 mg; a suicide attempt was the most common motive in 14 of the 20 studies that reported motive (37.3–98.7% of cases); a history of other substance use or dependence was reported in 5.3–45.9% and earlier tramadol misuse or dependence in 3.8–66.4%. The commonest features were nausea, vomiting and changes in consciousness. Table 5 lists only each series' three commonest other features: apnoea is among them in four series (4.7%, 15.0% in a paediatric series, 3.6% and 6.2%), and ICU admission is given for four series (0%, 7.0%, 1.0% and 20.6%). ['In the four series that gave it' implied that no other series recorded apnoea.]
key_findings.locator: Results › Seizure and mortality in tramadol poisoning, 1st paragraph (p. 23); Table 5 (pp. 15–19)

key_findings.finding: Death records: tramadol was the cause of death, as the review labels it, in a pooled 5.7% (95% CI 0.5–15.4; I2 97.6%) of drug-poisoning death records. National unpublished forensic data for 2016–17: 336 tramadol-related deaths among 2175 records of 'abusive drug-poisoning' fatalities (15.4%). In samples of 5000 forensic toxicology records a year, tramadol-related deaths rose from 4 (0.1%) in 2005 to 62 (1.2%), 98 (1.9%) and 130 (2.6%) in 2006–2008, with opioids also detected in 17 (27.4%), 50 (51%) and 41 (31.5%) of them. Tramadol was detected in 16 of 618 traffic deaths (2.6%), third after alcohol and morphine, and in 235 of 1274 methadone-associated deaths (18.5%), second after methamphetamine. [The card's wording read as if 336 of the 2175 records were 'abusive'; in Table 7 all 2175 are 'abusive' records and 336 are tramadol-related.]
key_findings.locator: Table 7 (p. 22); Results › Contribution of tramadol to death records, 1st paragraph (p. 23); Figure 7 (p. 23)
key_findings.note: Read from Figure 7 at 300 dpi: only 4 datasets are pooled (15.4%, 4.7%, 4.4% and 1.5%), the unpublished national dataset carrying 26% of the weight, with a prediction interval of 0–72.3%.

key_findings.finding: National adverse drug reaction data for 2006–10: 249 patients (117 men) with 461 reactions attributed to tramadol; reports fell from 89 in 2006 to 21 in 2010; seizure was the most reported reaction (29.3%), followed by nausea (22.5%), vomiting (18.8%) and vertigo (17.6%); three reactions (1.2% of patients) were fatal.
key_findings.locator: Results › Tramadol-related adverse drug reactions, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Nine Iranian case reports describe 10 patients (9 men): seizures in 9, including one after 200 mg by mouth with no other drug and two after intravenous use; two patients died, after oral ingestions reported as 10,000 mg and 14,000 mg.
key_findings.note: Case reports; they show that these events happened, not how often or at which amounts.

key_findings.finding: Of the 55 studies of tramadol poisoning and its consequences (Tables 3–6), none met all quality items and three met fewer than five; only one was national, the others covering 17 of 31 provinces (the seven forensic death studies, two of them national, are counted separately). The analysis was not preregistered and the authors call its results exploratory. ['Poisoning and mortality studies' with 'only one national' does not fit Table 3, which lists two national forensic datasets.]
key_findings.locator: Method › Data analysis, 1st paragraph (p. 2); Results › Tramadol-related poisoning, seizure and mortality, 1st paragraph (starting p. 20, continuing p. 21)

key_findings.finding: Stated limitations: few studies in some subgroups; prevalence studies in only eight of the 31 provinces; study year assessed only as a linear trend; tramadol often not asked about separately or not separated from medical use; no population-based survey of dependence (regular use used as a proxy); no longitudinal study of health outcomes of people using tramadol; and in some forensic studies no definite confirmation that tramadol was the only or main substance.
The Discussion states that in one year tramadol was found to be the sole cause of death in 336 cases [44] and that 71.0% of people seeking tramadol could get it without a prescription [39].
key_findings.note: Table 7 does not say that tramadol was the sole cause in the 336 records, and the Results give 58% for the same pharmacy study [39] (p. 14).

reporting_issues.issue: Ghasempouri 2014 is given as 5.9% of 17,390 all-cause poisoning admissions in Table 4 (p. 14) but as 0.008 (0.8%) in Figure 4 (p. 20); 0.8% matches the 137 tramadol-only cases of that study in Table 5 (p. 15).
reporting_issues.consequence: The 4.9% all-cause pool used 0.8% for its largest study; Table 4 cannot be used to reproduce the pool, and if Table 4 is right, that hospital's share is about seven times the value pooled (editors' arithmetic: 5.9% against 0.8%).

reporting_issues.issue: For Taremian 2014, Table 2 gives 3582 students (2285 men, 1246 women), while the forest plots give 1273 men (Figure 2) and 2300 women (Figure 3).
reporting_issues.consequence: The sexes' sample sizes appear swapped in one of the two places, which changes that study's weight in the student lifetime pools.

reporting_issues.issue: For Yaghoubi 2018 [28], past-month use (1.7% of men, 0.8% in total) is higher than past-year use (1.0% and 0.6%) in Table 2, which cannot happen in one sample.
reporting_issues.consequence: One of the two values is wrong; the past-year values enter the student pools.

reporting_issues.issue: Bashirian 2014 [26] and Fathi 2012 [30] share authors and city (Hamedan, three centres) and report the same sample size and sex split (400: 185 men, 215 women) and the same lifetime prevalence (12.5%), with study years given as 2012 and 2010; they are counted as two studies.
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably one sample reported twice; only Fathi enters the sex-specific pools (where women's 7.9% is an outlier), so the double count affects the study count and the student totals more than the pooled estimates.

reporting_issues.issue: Several pooled series come from the same city and overlapping periods: in Kermanshah, Ahmadi 2011 (2008–09, 546 patients), Ahmadi 2012 (March 2008–10, 1023) and Tatari 2010 (2008–09, 520); in Tehran, Talaie 2009 (April–September 2007, 132), Rashidi-Bonab 2017 (April–August 2007, 420) and Shadnia 2008 (April–May 2007 or 2008, 114). All are in the seizure pool. The review does not say whether their patients overlap.
reporting_issues.consequence: Patients may be counted more than once, narrowing the intervals; the two Ahmadi series from the same city and years give deaths of 0.9% and 10.0% (Figure 6), a difference the review does not discuss.

reporting_issues.issue: Seizure frequencies are said to range from 12.0% to 69.3% (p. 23), but the lowest pooled study is 11.7% in Figure 5 (11.6% in Table 5), and two series listed with seizure data in Table 5, a paediatric series with 0% and a series with 41.6%, are not in the pool, without explanation.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor for the pooled 34.6%, but the inclusion rule for the seizure pool is not stated.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says nineteen studies provided mortality rates (p. 23), while Figure 6 pools 18; per-study mortality appears nowhere except Figure 6 (Table 5 has no mortality column).
reporting_issues.consequence: The nineteenth study is probably the paediatric series with no deaths, but this is not stated; the death data cannot be checked against a table.

reporting_issues.issue: The pooled 13.1% share of drug-poisoning admissions, reported in the abstract (p. 1), comes from three studies whose values range from 7.1% to 20.3%, but Figure 4 gives no I2 and calls the prediction interval inestimable with fewer than 3 studies although three were pooled (p. 20); the general-population lifetime pools (three sites) show the same gap (p. 8).
reporting_issues.consequence: The heterogeneity behind a headline estimate is not reported; the estimate should be cited with its range of study values.

reporting_issues.issue: The death-record section says seven studies provided data (p. 23), but only four datasets are pooled in Figure 7; the pooled 5.7% is pulled up by an unpublished national dataset (15.4%, against 1.5–4.7% for the other three; the four weights are nearly equal, 23–26%), with a prediction interval of 0–72.3%.
reporting_issues.consequence: The pooled 5.7% is barely informative and leans on data that have not been peer reviewed; it should be cited with the individual datasets. ['Driven by ... 26% of the weight' overstated the weight, which matches the others.]

reporting_issues.issue: The general-population sample sizes are said to range from 403 to 3580 (p. 7), but the largest sample in Table 2 is 3508 (p. 6); the stated total of 12,783 matches 3508.
The text says males predominated in all poisoning and seizure studies (p. 23), but Table 5 includes a series of 38 women (p. 15) and a series of 54 patients with 27 men and 27 women (p. 17).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor overstatement; the predominance of men is general but not universal.

reporting_issues.issue: The meta-regression reports lifetime prevalence as significantly lower than past-year prevalence (P=0.02, p. 7), which cannot hold within any population; the regression table is only in Data S5.
reporting_issues.consequence: The study-level model is confounded by differences between studies (for example indirect estimation methods in the past-year studies) or the direction is misreported; its other null findings should be read with that in mind.

reporting_issues.issue: Study details differ between tables and figures: Shadnia 2008 is dated April–May 2008 in Table 3 (p. 12), April and May 2007 in Table 4 (p. 14) and 2007 in Table 5 (p. 16); Rashidi-Bonab 2017 is placed in Tehran in Tables 3 and 5 and in Eastern Azarbayjan in Figures 5 and 6 (p. 21); in Table 5, Taheri 2018 has 81.1% both as suicide attempt and as therapeutic use (with 18.9% unintentional), and one row prints the reference numbers [105] and [106] in place of percentages (pp. 15, 18–19).
reporting_issues.consequence: Transcription errors in the extracted data; they weaken confidence in the tables but do not change the headline pools as far as can be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: For the same pharmacy study [39], the Results say 58% asked for tramadol without a prescription (p. 14) and the Discussion says 71.0% could get it without a prescription (p. 24).
reporting_issues.consequence: The two figures may measure different things, but the paper does not reconcile them; the Results figure should be cited.

disagreements.first_pass: In the 34 poisoning and seizure series, mean age ranged from 22.0 to 28.4 years and mean reported ingested amount from 363.2 to 3248 mg; a suicide attempt was the most common motive in 14 of the 20 studies that reported motive (37.3–98.7% of cases); a history of other substance use or dependence was reported in 5.3–45.9% and earlier tramadol misuse or dependence in 3.8–66.4%. The commonest features were nausea, vomiting and changes in consciousness. Apnoea was recorded in 4.7%, 15.0% (a paediatric series), 3.6% and 6.2% in the four series that gave it, and ICU admission in 0%, 7.0%, 1.0% and 20.6% in four series.
disagreements.reviewer: In the 34 poisoning and seizure series, mean age ranged from 22.0 to 28.4 years and mean reported ingested amount from 363.2 to 3248 mg; a suicide attempt was the most common motive in 14 of the 20 studies that reported motive (37.3–98.7% of cases); a history of other substance use or dependence was reported in 5.3–45.9% and earlier tramadol misuse or dependence in 3.8–66.4%. The commonest features were nausea, vomiting and changes in consciousness. Table 5 lists only each series' three commonest other features: apnoea is among them in four series (4.7%, 15.0% in a paediatric series, 3.6% and 6.2%), and ICU admission is given for four series (0%, 7.0%, 1.0% and 20.6%). ['In the four series that gave it' implied that no other series recorded apnoea.]
disagreements.resolution: Second reader's correction adopted by the AI co-editor (AI reader 771 (round-2 check))

disagreements.first_pass: Death records: tramadol was the cause of death, as the review labels it, in a pooled 5.7% (95% CI 0.5–15.4; I2 97.6%) of drug-poisoning death records. National unpublished forensic data for 2016–17: 336 of 2175 drug-poisoning death records classed as 'abusive' (15.4%). In samples of 5000 forensic toxicology records a year, tramadol-related deaths rose from 4 (0.1%) in 2005 to 62 (1.2%), 98 (1.9%) and 130 (2.6%) in 2006–2008, with opioids also detected in 17 (27.4%), 50 (51%) and 41 (31.5%) of them. Tramadol was detected in 16 of 618 traffic deaths (2.6%), third after alcohol and morphine, and in 235 of 1274 methadone-associated deaths (18.5%), second after methamphetamine.
disagreements.reviewer: Death records: tramadol was the cause of death, as the review labels it, in a pooled 5.7% (95% CI 0.5–15.4; I2 97.6%) of drug-poisoning death records. In samples of 5000 forensic toxicology records a year, tramadol-related deaths rose from 4 (0.1%) in 2005 to 62 (1.2%), 98 (1.9%) and 130 (2.6%) in 2006–2008, with opioids also detected in 17 (27.4%), 50 (51%) and 41 (31.5%) of them. Tramadol was detected in 16 of 618 traffic deaths (2.6%), third after alcohol and morphine, and in 235 of 1274 methadone-associated deaths (18.5%), second after methamphetamine. [The card's wording read as if 336 of the 2175 records were 'abusive'; in Table 7 all 2175 are 'abusive' records and 336 are tramadol-related.]
